sens: Aquatic plant with flexible, hollow stems that grows in wet and marshy areas
Rope or woven object made from the fibers of this plant
That which is weak, humble, or insignificant
That which collapses or bends under weight
Attitude of humility or submission, symbolized by bending
H0100.detail:
1. The reed is a common aquatic plant with soft, hollow stems; the Bible mentions it to refer to woven or twisted objects. In Job 40:21, the "reed" in the nostrils of Leviathan remains a mystery for translators — perhaps a shape or object, but mainly a symbol of the wildest and most untamed creature.
2. Its fibers were used to make flexible ropes, utensils, or "boilers" — vessels that can boil (Job 41:11), evoking the idea of something flexible, capable of containing, but also of transforming.
3. In the prophecies of Isaiah, the reed metaphorically represents the small, weak, and insignificant of Israel and Egypt, in contrast to the "palm branch" (the great, the powerful). In Isaiah 9:13 and 19:15, God will "pull up" the reed, symbolizing the elimination of the weak.
4. The reed, as a plant that naturally bends, becomes the image of bending and lowering. It is a passive, flexible, obedient posture.
5. In Isaiah 58:5, "bending the head like a reed" depicts the humility of fasting: the body that bends, inclines, submits — a posture of a humble heart before God.
H0100.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of flexibility and lowering. Its primary meaning refers to the actual plant, common in the marshes of the Near East; but it quickly shifts to the image of bending and weakness. The physical flexibility of the reed makes it a natural symbol of humility and non-resistance.
H0100.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in a symbolic context rather than a botanical one. In the descriptions of Leviathan (Job 40:21 and 41:11), it retains a shade of concrete reality, even if obscure. In Isaiah, especially in prophetic context, it becomes a figure of the weak and despised: those who bend before the powerful, or those who are crushed. In Isaiah 58:5, the bent reed becomes the language of the body in authentic fasting — the physical expression of repentance and submission to God.
H0100.portee: The reed teaches that weakness and humility are not defects to be hated, but postures before God. God cares about the bent reed, the heart that humbles itself (Isaiah 58:5), far more than about pompous appearances. This image reminds us that true strength lies in flexibility, obedience, and the absence of proud rigidity — a lesson for the Christian seeking to bow before the Lord.

sens: Hollow container used to hold or pour liquids
Rounded shape, elegant curve of a part of the body
Set of descendants or members of a family
H0101.detail:
1. The basin is a hollow container, a cup used to hold or manipulate liquids, especially in religious rites: in Exodus 24:6, Moses puts the blood of the sacrifice in it for the sprinkling of the altar.
2. By its hollow and rounded aspect, the word also designates the elegant curves of the human body, particularly the chest: in Song of Solomon 7:3, the well-formed chest of the beloved is compared to a basin containing fragrant wine, an image of a harmonious and attractive shape.
3. By metaphorical extension, the basin signifies the entire set of descendants or dependents of a household, its "offspring": in Isaiah 22:24, the house of his father extends like a basin overflowing with its numerous descendants, small or large.
H0101.origine: The Hebrew word aggan comes from a root evoking a hollow, rounded, or bulging shape. Its basic image is that of a hollow, a cavity capable of holding. In Greek, this word is rendered by the term liknis or by words designating vessels and containers. The family of Hebrew words around this root explores the idea of rounded, concave, or overflowing shapes.
H0101.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. It first designates a concrete utensil of worship: the basin that receives the blood of sacrifices during the Sinai ceremony (Exodus 24:6). It is then used in the love poetry of the Song of Solomon to evoke physical beauty, the graceful roundness of a chest (7:3). Finally, it takes a fixed, almost metaphorical meaning to designate the abundant descendants of a household (Isaiah 22:24), where the basin becomes the image of a family overflowing with many offspring. The word thus shifts from the concrete to the sensitive, then to the figurative.
H0101.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hesitate to describe the human body with respect and poetry, celebrating its beauty. It also shows how a simple word, that of a worship container, enriches the poetic and symbolic language of faith: the utensils of the sanctuary become images of the beloved body and of divine blessing in descendants.

sens: Group of soldiers forming a military unit
Division of an army, detachment
Body of warriors grouped for a common action
Multitude of armed people or in movement
H0102.detail:
1. A troop is an organized group of soldiers who fight together under the same command. In Ezekiel 38:9, the prophet sees Gog attacking "like a storm" with "all your troops," meaning all of his coordinated military forces.
2. The word also designates a division or section of a larger army, an autonomous detachment. When Ezekiel 17:21 speaks of the "fugitives from all his troops" who fall by the sword, it evokes the scattered remnants of combat groups that have been defeated.
3. More broadly, a troop is any grouping of warriors or fighters acting together, even without a strict military structure. In Ezekiel 38:22, God's judgments fall upon Gog "and upon his troops, and upon the many peoples who will be with him": this is the entire mass of assembled warriors.
4. The word can also evoke a multitude in motion, a large crowd of armed people or those ready for battle, particularly in a context of invasion or military mobilization.
H0102.origine: The Hebrew word אֲגַף (agaph) probably comes from a root meaning the action of gathering or grouping. The fundamental meaning is that of a "wing" or a "formation" — like the wing of an army on the battlefield. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), this word is often rendered by a term meaning "side" or "part" of an army. The image is that of warriors gathering and tightening to form a compact and mobile force.
H0102.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the prophet Ezekiel, in chapters 12, 17, and 38-39. It always designates military forces in a context of divine judgment upon the nations. Ezekiel uses it to speak of the army of King Zedekiah that is scattered (12:14, 17:21), and then especially of the immense coalition of Gog that invades Israel (38:6, 38:9, 38:22, 39:4). In all these cases, the "troop" is a group of warriors that will either be scattered or destroyed by the judgment of the Lord. The word reinforces the idea of an organized force standing against God and His people.
H0102.portee: This word reminds the reader that God rules over all military powers, no matter how organized and numerous they may be. Even the most formidable troops, assembled in great numbers, cannot withstand divine judgment. For the believer, it is an assurance that no one, no human or enemy force, can annihilate the people of God without facing the Lord Himself.

sens: to gather and pile up things in large quantities
to accumulate provisions or resources for future days
to gather the fruits of a harvest
H0103.detail:
1. Amasser means to gather and pile up: it is the action of putting together a large quantity of something. It is concrete: one stacks, one accumulates (Proverbs 6:8: the ant "gathers" during the harvest, meaning it collects and stores grain).
2. The word especially evokes the accumulation of provisions for the future: one gathers to have something to eat later, one prepares a reserve (Proverbs 10:5: "He who gathers in summer is a wise son," he thinks of winter).
3. In the agricultural context, to gather means to harvest and collect: it is the fruit of labor in the fields (Deuteronomy 28:39: you will not make a "harvest" — literally, you will not gather — because the locusts will eat your vines).
H0103.origine: The Hebrew root agar evokes the action of gathering in heaps. It belongs to the family of words related to accumulation and collection. The verb is commonly used to describe the harvest and storage of goods, particularly in wisdom texts that focus on the prudent management of resources.
H0103.emploi: The verb appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible, all usages provided. It is characteristic of the vocabulary of harvest and foresight: in Deuteronomy 28:39, in a blessing and curse, it describes what the farmer will not be able to do if God curses him; in Proverbs 6:8 and 10:5, it illustrates the wisdom of one who works in summer to anticipate winter or a bad season. It is a practical word, rooted in agricultural life and the morality of the Old Testament.
H0103.portee: Gathering teaches that foresight is not a fault but a virtue. The wise person accumulates, prepares, thinks of tomorrow — this is what distinguishes him from one who sleeps or wastes. But the word also reminds us that every harvest is a gift from God: one gathers only if God allows it, and the loss of harvest is His judgment.

sens: Written message intended to be sent to someone
Official or administrative document bearing an authority's decision
H0104.detail:
1. A letter is a written message sent over a distance to communicate with someone. It is the means of transmitting information, requests, or orders when one cannot speak in person. In Ezra 4:8, Rehum and Shimshai write a letter to King Artaxerxes to report problems concerning Jerusalem: it is an official written communication sent to a distant authority.
2. A letter can also refer to an official document bearing authority: a written statement signed by a person in a position of power, which becomes a sort of written decision or order. In Ezra 5:6, the copy of the letter sent to King Darius by Tattenai, the governor, is mentioned: it is an administrative document that carries authority and can be copied for archiving or record-keeping.
H0104.origine: The Aramaic word אִגְּרָא comes from the same root as the Hebrew אִגֶּרֶת (igguèreth), both derived from a basic image related to writing and transmission. It is a word specific to the later books of the Old Testament, notably Ezra, where Persian rule made the use of official written communications common. The Aramaic word reflects the historical context of these accounts: after the exile, the Judeans live under Persian administration and communicate with the authorities in writing.
H0104.emploi: The word appears only three times in Ezra (4:8, 4:11, 5:6), all usages concerning communications between Persian authorities and the government of Jerusalem. In Ezra 4:8-11, Rehum and Shimshai write a letter to King Artaxerxes to report that the Judeans are rebuilding the Temple, which disrupts the established order. In Ezra 5:6, it is Tattenai who sends a letter to King Darius. These three occurrences show that the word is strictly used for official documents of the Persian administration, never for private or personal correspondence. It is an administrative and political term.
H0104.portee: This word reminds the reader that the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile takes place under Persian oversight, through formal bureaucratic channels. The letters mentioned here show how opposition to God's plans goes through official procedures, and how God governs despite the political and administrative obstacles that earthly authorities place in the way of His people.

sens: Shallow, wide, and open container used to hold liquids or other materials
In a cultic context, sacred vessel of the Temple for ablutions or offerings
H0105.detail:
1. The basin is a widely open, shallow container made to hold water or other substances — the image is that of a flat, flared cup rather than a closed jug. In Ezra 1:9, Ezra lists the treasures of the restored Temple: among the gold and silver vessels offered for worship, the basins are mentioned alongside knives and other utensils, testifying to their ritual importance.
2. In the Temple of Jerusalem, the basin was a sacred object used for ritual ablutions (to purify with water) or to collect the blood of sacrifices. These vessels were made of gold or silver according to their rank in the worship, and were among the most precious goods of the sanctuary.
H0105.origine: The Aramaic word אֲגַרְטָל likely comes from an ancient Semitic root related to the idea of containing or carrying. The form suggests a borrowing from a neighboring language — perhaps Persian or a language of the ancient Levant — reflecting the cultural contacts of the Near East. This type of vessel was common in religious contexts throughout the Mediterranean and Near Eastern regions.
H0105.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 1:9, in the account of the return from exile and the reconstruction of the Temple. Ezra lists the sacred vessels that King Cyrus has released for the Jews to bring back to Jerusalem. This unique mention shows that the basin was an important object of Temple worship, worthy of being inventoried among the most precious treasures — the text counts dozens in gold and thousands in silver.
H0105.portee: This passage reminds us of the preciousness of the worship rendered to God and the symbolic value of each object in the sanctuary. The basins, like all these vessels, were not mere utensils: they embodied the separation between the sacred and the profane, and their restoration marked the renewal of communion with God after the exile. For the believer, this underscores that even the most humble objects of worship carry spiritual dignity.

sens: Closed hand, clenched fist
Blow delivered with the fist
Act of violence or aggression
H0106.detail:
1. The fist is the hand closed with the fingers folded: it is the natural form of the hand ready to strike. In Exodus 21:18, in the law concerning quarrels, the fist is mentioned as the instrument of a fight between two men — one strikes the other with a stone or with the fist, which can cause serious injuries.
2. The fist also refers to the blow itself, the action of striking: it is by extension the physical violence exercised with closed fists. This appears in the same verse from Exodus where the impact of the fist is a legal fact that the law weighs the consequences of.
3. Isaiah 58:4 uses the expression "striking wickedly with the fist" to describe a malicious aggression, not in honest rebellion but with the intent to harm. The prophet reproaches the Israelites for fasting insincerely: they dispute and quarrel violently instead of seeking justice and peace.
H0106.origine: The Hebrew word אֶגְרֹף (egrouph) comes from a root that evokes the idea of closing, of tightening. The fist is literally the hand tightened, closed into a ball. This word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of the body and physical strength, common in accounts of confrontation or justice.
H0106.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It first appears in Exodus 21:18, in the covenant code, to define a type of blow during a quarrel — a legal case that the law must adjudicate. It reappears in Isaiah 58:4, where the prophet uses it to criticize false piety: fasting while fighting with the fist does not honor God. In both cases, the fist symbolizes a violent and brutal action, in rupture with the order or justice that God demands.
H0106.portee: The fist reminds us that physical violence has legal and moral consequences. In Exodus, the law even protects the one who fights: it does not ignore violence, it regulates it. In Isaiah, the prophet shows that an outward religion (fasting) that coexists with aggression towards others is a sham: God desires heart transformation, not the pious gestures of a violent person. It is a call to moral integrity and peace.

sens: written or message transmitted from one person to another
official document bearing authority (from the king, a leader)
written correspondence
H0107.detail:
1. A letter is a written message sent to someone to communicate information. Hezekiah "wrote letters" to invite Israel to celebrate Passover (2 Chronicles 30:1): an act of communication at a distance.
2. In a political or administrative context, the letter is primarily an official document endowed with authority. Nehemiah requests from the king "letters for the governors" (Nehemiah 2:7): these royal writings open doors and command obedience. It is an instrument of power.
3. The letter can also be a missive of threat or derision: Sanballat sends Nehemiah "an open letter" to intimidate him (Nehemiah 6:5). The word then designates any writing intended to influence or provoke a reaction from the recipient.
H0107.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of bending or folding (as one folds parchment or papyrus). The related Aramaic (igra) shows that this vocabulary was shared by the peoples of the Levant. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the corresponding Hebrew when the context speaks of official written communications.
H0107.emploi: This word appears 10 times, mainly in the later historical books (Nehemiah, Esther, 2 Chronicles). It almost always designates royal letters or those from high officials: Hezekiah summons Israel by letter (2 Chronicles 30:1, 30:6), Nehemiah obtains letters of passage from the Persian king (Nehemiah 2:7, 2:8, 2:9), Sanballat resorts to a letter to threaten (Nehemiah 6:5). In the book of Esther, the word reappears for the royal edicts concerning the Jews. Each time, the letter carries authority and compels obedience.
H0107.portee: This word reminds us that before electronics, writing was the only means to transmit authority at a distance and leave a trace. For the believer, this sheds light on how God also spoke through his servants and prophets: his word, like a royal letter, must be received and obeyed. It also highlights the importance of faithful communication in governance and collective life.

sens: Mist or cloud of moisture rising from the earth
Vapor or humidity that rises in fine suspension
H0108.detail: 1. The word designates a mist or a light cloud of moisture rising from the earth to water its surface: it is dew or water vapor in visible form. In Genesis 2:6, before God causes rain to fall, a vapor rises from the ground and moistens it — it is the natural irrigation mechanism that preserves vegetation. 2. The word also describes the process by which water transforms into fine invisible droplets that rise into the air to later form rain. In Job 36:27, God draws the drops of water and reduces them to vapor, demonstrating his dominion over the natural water cycle: it is an act of divine power.
H0108.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of something humid and elusive that rises. The word belongs to a simple and observational lexical field: it is the vocabulary of the farmer who sees the morning mist or the cloud forming. It describes a visible and elemental phenomenon, fundamental for agricultural life in the Middle East.
H0108.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 2:6, it appears in the creation narrative: God creates a world where vapor rises from the earth to sustain life. In Job 36:27, the wise Elihu uses it to show how God governs the water cycle with wisdom and power. In both cases, it is a natural phenomenon but of which God is the author and master.
H0108.portee: This simple word reminds us that God does not merely create once: he maintains every day the vital mechanisms that sustain creation. The vapor that rises, the water that circulates, the rain that nourishes — all of this is the work of his wisdom. It invites the believer to see in the daily natural phenomena the hands of God at work.

sens: Cause pain, moral distress to someone
Experience deep sadness oneself
Afflict, overwhelm someone with grief
H0109.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the action of causing sorrow to someone, inflicting a heartache. This is what God does in speaking to Eli: he will allow one of his descendants to survive, but "sadden" his soul, meaning to make him experience deep sorrow at seeing the death of others (1 Samuel 2:33).
2. The word can also refer to the feeling of sadness experienced by the one who suffers this pain: to be moved, afflicted, morally downcast.
3. In its strongest usage, "sadden" means to ravage someone with pain, to consume them with grief to the point of completely overwhelming them.
H0109.origine: The Hebrew word אָדַב comes from a root that expresses the idea of deep pain and affliction. It is akin to the state of a person who is overwhelmed by sorrow, who loses their momentum and strength under the weight of despair. The verb is generally used in the causative form (Hiph): not merely to be sad, but to cause sadness in others.
H0109.emploi: The verb אָדַב appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 2:33, in God's judgment against Eli the priest. God announces that he will allow one of his descendants to live, but he "saddened" him by seeing him deprived of offspring and full of bitterness. Thus, it is a term reserved for a moment of serious divine judgment, expressing how God afflicts the one who has offended him. The unique usage underscores the dramatic weight of this judgment.
H0109.portee: This word reveals how God's judgment is not mere destruction: it can be a persistent affliction, a heartache inflicted on one who has disobeyed. For the believer, this shows that distance from God is a source of deep sadness, and that divine discipline touches the soul above all. It is also a reminder that God sees the heart and knows all its pains.

sens: son of Ishmael and grandson of Abraham
member of the genealogy of Arab peoples
H0110.detail:
1. Adbeel is one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, listed alongside his brothers such as Kedar, Nebajoth, and others (Genesis 25:13). He represents a branch of Abraham's descendants through his son Ishmael.
2. He embodies the genealogy of the Arab peoples of antiquity. The genealogical lists in the Bible trace the origins of the neighboring peoples of Israel and show how all human beings descend from a common root (1 Chronicles 1:29).
H0110.origine: The name Adbeel literally means "punished by God" or "God has punished" (from ad = punish and el = God in Hebrew). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name, which was common among ancient Arabs. The name expresses a relationship to God, although its exact historical context is unknown to us.
H0110.emploi: Adbeel appears twice in the Bible, always in genealogical lists: in Genesis 25:13 as the third son of Ishmael, and in 1 Chronicles 1:29 as a confirmation of this genealogy. These lists serve to establish the origins of the Arab peoples contemporary to the patriarchs. Adbeel is never mentioned individually in a narrative or specific event, but only as a link in the genealogical chain connecting Abraham to his distant descendants.

sens: Young Edomite prince who fled to Egypt
Enemy that God raised against Solomon
H0111.detail:
1. Hadad was a young prince of the kingdom of Edom who fled to Egypt with his father's servants to escape the rule of David and Solomon (1 Kings 11:17). There he found refuge and was welcomed by the Pharaoh, whose sister he would marry.
2. God used Hadad as an instrument of punishment against Solomon: after the king turned away from the Lord by marrying foreign women and worshiping their gods, Scripture tells us that God raised up Hadad as an adversary to remind Solomon of the cost of his unfaithfulness.
H0111.origine: The name Hadad means "I will move gently" or "I will love," according to an ancient Semitic etymology. This name was borne by several important figures in the ancient Near East, including gods of Syrian worship. Here, Hadad is a historical Edomite figure whose fate illustrates how God uses political events in the Middle East to judge the unfaithfulness of His people.
H0111.emploi: Hadad is mentioned only once by name in the provided text (1 Kings 11:17), but the account concerning him extends over several verses in chapter 11 of 1 Kings. He is a young boy at the time of his flight to Egypt. Solomon made him a formidable adversary who, once grown, harassed him during his reign. His story illustrates how God's punishments against His chosen people can take the form of rivals raised against unfaithful kings.
H0111.portee: The story of Hadad teaches the reader that God judges royal unfaithfulness and that there are no insignificant consequences in abandoning the covenant with the Lord. It also shows that even a fleeing child can become, years later, an instrument of divine correction.

sens: Israeli leader at the return from Babylonian exile
H0112.detail: Iddo is an Israeli leader mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return of the exiles from Babylon. He lived in Casiphia, a location not otherwise identified, and was responsible for a community that included the Nethinim (temple servants). Ezra sent him to seek men to serve in the house of God in the rebuilt Jerusalem (Ezra 8:17).
H0112.origine: The name Iddo means "I will praise him" or "the one who is praised," formed from the Hebrew root expressing praise. It is a theophoric name, meaning it includes a relationship to God and expresses trust in His goodness.
H0112.emploi: Iddo is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in Ezra 8:17. He appears during Ezra's mission to reconstitute the temple's workforce after the return from captivity. His role suggests that he was a man of influence and trust, capable of mobilizing the temple servants who remained in Mesopotamia and directing them to Jerusalem.

sens: One who commands, who has authority over others; master of a house or estate.
Husband, spouse in a marital relationship.
King, sovereign who reigns over a people.
God, the Lord of the universe and all creation.
Title of respect, form of politeness towards someone superior or important.
Figure of spiritual authority, such as a prophet or an angel.
H0113.detail:
1. The lord is primarily one who directs, who commands: a master of a house or one who manages a property, its affairs, and its servants. In Genesis 24, Abraham's servant constantly speaks of his master's role in his daily life (Genesis 24:12, 24:36).

2. The word designates the husband in the couple: the wife recognizes in him one who has authority. In Psalm 45:12, the queen honors the king as her lord.

3. A lord can be a king, a sovereign who reigns over a territory or a people (Deuteronomy 10:17 speaks of the Lord God, "who shows no partiality").

4. The word applies primarily to God Himself: the Lord of the entire universe, the one who has absolute authority (Joshua 5:14, where Joshua encounters the lord of the Lord's army).

5. It is also a formula of respect and politeness: it is used towards someone one honors or depends on, as Abraham towards the three visitors in Genesis 18:3.

6. Sometimes it designates a spiritual authority: a prophet, an angel, or any being recognized as superior, before whom one bows.
H0113.origine: The Hebrew word אָדוֹן comes from a root expressing strength and solidity. Its primary image is that of a firm, established person, capable of holding a position of authority. The family of the word includes various forms that reinforce the idea of command and mastery. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word is generally rendered by κύριος (kurios, "lord"), the same term found in the New Testament to designate Jesus as Lord.
H0113.emploi: The word lord appears about 285 times in the Old Testament. It is extremely frequent in the account of Joseph, where it qualifies Potiphar, Joseph's Egyptian master, or where Joseph himself is called lord by those who obey him (Genesis 39-40). It is omnipresent in the relationships between masters and servants (Exodus 21), between kings and subjects, and between husbands and wives (Exodus 21:4-5). Applied to God, it becomes "the Lord" par excellence, surpassing all other lords (Deuteronomy 10:17). Its meaning varies little: it is always one who has authority, but the relationship changes according to the context — servant to an earthly master, creature to God, or wife to her husband.
H0113.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on authority and submission. For a believer, recognizing God as Lord means bowing before His will and absolute command. But it also reminds us that lordship carries a responsibility: a good lord, like God, cares for those under His authority. It is a key word for understanding how the Bible envisions the relationship between the Creator and His creation, and between human beings in their relationships of authority and service.
